quote: stop all dopamine antagonists immediately (and restart any withdrawn dopaminergic therapy if that was the trigger);
problem: The all-severity first step in a case built on a confounded medication list stops only the D2 antagonists; nothing on the page says to hold the recently up-titrated venlafaxine while serotonin toxicity is still on the differential.
whyItMatters: A resident following the ladder literally keeps a febrile (39.4 °C), rigid, confused patient on an escalated SNRI; if the syndrome is (or includes) serotonin toxicity, continued exposure sustains it, and there is no cost to holding it during the workup.
evidence: Boyer & Shannon, N Engl J Med 2005;352:1112-20 (page ref 2): discontinuation of all serotonergic agents is the first step in serotonin syndrome; Tormoehlen & Rusyniak, Handb Clin Neurol 2018 (ref 5): when NMS and SS cannot be separated, withdraw both classes of precipitant.
correction: stop all dopamine antagonists immediately (and restart any withdrawn dopaminergic therapy if that was the trigger); hold venlafaxine and any other serotonergic agent until serotonin toxicity is excluded;

problem: Bromocriptine is recommended without the standard caution that it has serotonergic activity and has been associated with worsened (including fatal) outcomes when serotonin syndrome was misdiagnosed as NMS — the exact confusion this case is built around.
whyItMatters: In a patient who is also on a recently increased SNRI, a resident may start bromocriptine before serotonin toxicity is reasonably excluded, which can worsen the syndrome the case explicitly keeps on the differential.
evidence: Boyer EW, Shannon M. N Engl J Med 2005;352:1112-20 (the page's ref 2): bromocriptine is contraindicated in serotonin syndrome and has been implicated in fatal outcomes when SS was misdiagnosed as NMS.
correction: consider **bromocriptine** (2.5 mg q8h, titrated) or **amantadine** — only once serotonin toxicity is reasonably excluded, because bromocriptine can worsen serotonin syndrome

quote: continue dopamine agonists ≥10 days after resolution to avoid rebound, given depot/long half-life exposures
problem: The duration rule is garbled: the conventional guidance is ~10 days after resolution following oral antipsychotics and 2–3 weeks after depot exposure, but the sentence attaches the 10-day figure to depot/long-half-life exposure.
whyItMatters: A resident managing depot-associated NMS could stop bromocriptine/amantadine at 10 days while the depot is still releasing drug, risking rebound NMS.
evidence: Strawn JR, Keck PE Jr, Caroff SN. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Am J Psychiatry 2007;164:870-6: continue dopaminergic treatment ~10 days after resolution for oral agents and 2–3 weeks after depot antipsychotics.
correction: continue dopamine agonists ~10 days after resolution (2–3 weeks after depot or other long-half-life exposure) to avoid rebound

quote: Intubation and paralysis if refractory hyperthermia.
problem: Paralysis (and, in the next bullet, ECT) is recommended in a patient with CK >28,000, myoglobinuria and rising creatinine without stating that succinylcholine must be avoided and a non-depolarizing agent used.
whyItMatters: The psychiatry resident often hands this patient to ICU/anesthesia or consents for ECT; succinylcholine in rhabdomyolysis risks hyperkalemic cardiac arrest, and the caution belongs in the plan that travels with the patient.
evidence: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalemia risk (succinylcholine US label, warnings); Boyer & Shannon 2005 (ref 2) specify non-depolarizing paralysis for hyperthermic serotonin toxicity. Same defect class as prior finding RV11-F010 on the earlier (2026-07-09) SS/NMS case.
correction: Intubation and paralysis with a non-depolarizing agent if refractory hyperthermia — avoid succinylcholine (rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalemia), a caution that also travels with any ECT referral.

quote: usually clears within 24–48 h of drug cessation [2,3].
problem: Reference 8 (Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria) is listed but never cited, and a page titled SS vs NMS gives no diagnostic rule or treatment for serotonin toxicity (benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine) at all.
whyItMatters: A resident leaves an SS-vs-NMS conference without the standard clonus-based decision rule or the specific SS treatment, and the reference list implies support the text never draws on.
evidence: Dunkley EJC et al. QJM 2003;96:635-42 (Hunter criteria; ref 8); Boyer & Shannon NEJM 2005 (ref 2): management = stop agent, supportive care, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine for moderate–severe cases.
correction: usually clears within 24–48 h of drug cessation with supportive care, benzodiazepines and, if moderate–severe, cyproheptadine; the Hunter criteria (clonus-based) are the standard diagnostic rule [2,3,8].

quote: Keep documentation at the level of recognition, protective factors, and escalation thresholds.
problem: Q7 has the resident rehearse suicide-risk assessment and an ED discharge disposition with a written safety plan naming 'crisis resources', but the page carries no injected crisis block (the BPD case in this chunk does).
whyItMatters: Under the library's own policy a page doing disposition/safety-planning work must opt in to the crisis block; without it the resident building the safety plan has no vetted crisis contacts to put in it.
evidence: Standing editorial policy 2 (crisis contacts build-injected on pages doing real risk work); compare cotw_20260827_bpd_res.md, which carries the block.
correction:
Keep documentation at the level of recognition, protective factors, and escalation thresholds.

quote: any taper should be slow, collaborative, and paired with early-warning-sign monitoring and rapid re-engagement plans [3].
problem: The relapse-prevention discussion for a first-episode patient with poor insight never mentions offering a long-acting injectable antipsychotic, which the APA guideline supports and which has direct trial evidence in early-phase illness.
whyItMatters: Residents learn a first-episode maintenance plan that omits the one intervention shown to cut relapse/hospitalization in early illness, perpetuating the practice of reserving LAIs for chronic, multiply relapsed patients.
evidence: APA Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia 2020 (Keepers et al., ref 3), statement 10 (2B): LAI if the patient prefers it or has poor/uncertain adherence; PRELAPSE (Kane JM et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2020;77:1217-24): aripiprazole once-monthly reduced time to first hospitalization in early-phase schizophrenia.
correction: any taper should be slow, collaborative, and paired with early-warning-sign monitoring and rapid re-engagement plans [3]. Offer a long-acting injectable as a choice, not a punishment — the APA guideline supports it when the patient prefers it or adherence is uncertain, and early-phase trial evidence (PRELAPSE, 2020) shows fewer hospitalizations.

quote: catatonic patients usually lack capacity, so involve surrogate consent per jurisdiction, and know your local emergency-treatment pathway.
problem: Implies ECT for an incapacitated patient proceeds on surrogate consent; in many US states a health-care agent, family member or even guardian cannot consent to ECT without specific court authorization.
whyItMatters: A resident outside the author's state may plan ECT on next-of-kin consent and lose days (or act unlawfully) in a malignant-catatonia case where speed matters; the learner-facing teaching point should name the court-authorization possibility (the facilitator notes already ask the question).
evidence: e.g., Texas Estates Code §1151.054 (guardian may not consent to convulsive treatment); California Welf. & Inst. Code §5326.7 (conservator consent to ECT requires court determination); state law varies widely.
correction: catatonic patients usually lack capacity; know your state's substitute-consent rule for ECT — in many states a surrogate or even a guardian cannot consent to ECT without court authorization — and know your local emergency-treatment pathway.

quote: here mutism/verbigeration, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echopraxia, staring on the BFCRS
problem: The list counted toward DSM-5-TR's 12 signs includes verbigeration and staring, which are BFCRS items but not DSM-5-TR catatonia signs.
whyItMatters: Learners conflate the BFCRS item set with the DSM criterion list and may count non-DSM signs toward the ≥3 threshold in a borderline case.
evidence: DSM-5-TR catatonia criteria: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia.
correction: here mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and echopraxia; verbigeration and staring are additional BFCRS signs

quote: guideline-consistent practice reserves medication for discrete comorbid disorders and time-limited crisis use (low-dose antipsychotic or sedative antihistamine preferred;
problem: 'Guideline-consistent practice' is supported only by reviews [1,6,7]; the current US guideline — APA Practice Guideline for BPD (2024) — is not cited anywhere on the page, and the crisis-drug preference comes from NICE CG78, not APA.
whyItMatters: Residents cannot trace the pharmacotherapy position to the governing US guideline (which advises against pharmacotherapy as the primary intervention and supports reviewing/reducing polypharmacy), weakening the page's deprescribing argument.
evidence: Keepers GA et al. APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Borderline Personality Disorder. Am J Psychiatry 2024;181(11):1024-1028, doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.24181010 (PMID 39482953); NICE CG78 (2009).
correction: guideline-consistent practice (APA 2024 BPD guideline: pharmacotherapy not the primary intervention, with review and reduction of polypharmacy; NICE CG78: short-term crisis use only) reserves medication for discrete comorbid disorders and time-limited crisis use (low-dose antipsychotic or sedative antihistamine preferred;
verified: PubMed metadata PMID 39482953 (existence/citation); statement content from recall

quote: GPM performed comparably to DBT in the principal head-to-head trial and is designed for dissemination to general psychiatrists and residents [8].
problem: The trial result is attributed to a 2024 narrative review [8]; the head-to-head RCT itself (McMain et al., 2009) is not cited.
whyItMatters: A resident asked for the evidence cannot find the trial; the claim reads as resting on commentary rather than an RCT.
evidence: McMain SF, Links PS, Gnam WH, et al. A randomized trial of dialectical behavior therapy versus general psychiatric management for borderline personality disorder. Am J Psychiatry 2009;166(12):1365-74.
correction: GPM performed comparably to DBT in the principal head-to-head trial (McMain et al., Am J Psychiatry 2009) and is designed for dissemination to general psychiatrists and residents [8].
